newsitem.title: Malaysia: Foreign relocations seen hurting Malaysian industry.
newsitem.headline: Foreign relocations seen hurting Malaysian industry.

text.p: Multinational electronics firms are beginning to relocate from Malaysia to countries with cheaper labour, leaving behind a bruised local industry, businessmen and analysts said.

Local industry has yet to assimilate the high technology used by multinationals and with production costs rising, they, too, may have to close down or move to countries such as China, Thailand and the Philippines.

"Unless local companies increase automation or diversify into other cheaper markets, they could face some serious problems of survival," said an analyst with a Penang-based securities company in an interview.
"Many of them (local firms) have not gone beyond being suppliers to multinationals," the analyst said.

He said the problem was not yet acute because the northern island of Penang, dubbed "Malaysia's Silicon Valley", had a two-decade track record in the business, excellent infrastructure and skilled workers.
Some local manufacturers say they would be in trouble unless there was a concerted effort to upgrade technology, initiate product development and move to newer markets.

"From here we have to be able to capitalise on acquired knowledge, come up with new product derivatives, service derivatives," said Alfred Eong Liang Teh, managing director of Eng Teknologi Holdings Bhd.

"We have to think global. We have to at least think in terms of regionalisation. Believe me, this will be the only way to survive in the future," said Teh, whose company makes actuators for computer hard disk drives.
He said Malaysian companies may not yet be capable of any large-scale research and development, but they have to be able to at least develop new products.

Malaysia's electronics industry, the bulk of which is located in Penang, largely comprises multinational companies that set up over the last quarter-century due to growing costs in Japan, Europe and the United States.
A large local electronic products and components industry was spawned by the arrival of the multinationals. There are 34 local electronics companies in Penang.
"We started with the fact that the multinationals were here and they require parts, they require job works (to be done). That is the path (by which) most Penang companies have evolved," Teh said.
But, with wages increasing at 10-15 percent a year and skilled labour in short supply, Eng itself has invested in two plants in China and the Philippines to make actuators.
"As the multinationals go, any new product and expansion will not be here. That is why companies like us will have to think about realignment, movement," Teh said.
But the Penang state government says that with the base already established, multinationals will use higher technology to replace labour-intensive operations here.
"It is true we are no longer a cheap labour centre," Penang Chief Minister Koh Tsu Koon said in an interview last week.
"But the nature of the industry has also changed because they have moved to greater automation. And the skill content of our workforce has also changed," he said.

"We are undergoing a transition that Singapore and Hong Kong underwent a few years ago successfully. If we do our job well we will also undergo a successful transformation." He said investment by Penang-based companies remained high, citing a survey of 353 major factories that showed reinvestment totalled three billion ringgit in 1996.
